newsitem.title: INDIA: India considers intermediaries for stock lending.
newsitem.headline: India considers intermediaries for stock lending.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) is considering authorising the creation of financial intermediaries as part of a proposed stock lending scheme, a senior government official said on Wednesday.
"Financial institutions can make money on this," said the official, who asked not to be identified.
The stock market regulator's board was scheduled to meet in Bombay on Thursday to consider among other things the stock lending scheme, SEBI officials said in Bombay.
The meeting was also scheduled to discuss an amendment in the country's share depository law and a report on short sales.
The stock lending scheme, if approved, would involve the authorisation of intermediaries which could lend stocks to help share deliveries for a specificed financial return, the source said.

Under the proposed scheme, authorised institutions could lend their shares, which would have to be returned later to them in the same quantities, but the returned shares would not have to bear the same distinctive numbers, the source said.
Authorised institutions which have large quantities of shares could gain from this scheme by lending them for fixed returns to help meet delivery commitments by others, the official said.
SEBI chairman D.R. Mehta met Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia on Wednesday in New Delhi ahead of the board meeting on Thursday.

"I can't comment anything on that," Mehta told Reuters when asked to comment on Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's statement earlier this week that the government was considering a package to boost the capital market this week.
Deve Gowda had said in Bombay on Monday that some decisions could be expected before he left on Friday for Davos in Switzerland to attend a meeting of the World Economic Forum.
